Scans workloads and container images for known CVEs and exposure
Finds sensitive data such as PII and credentials inside S3 buckets
Builds a behaviour graph so an analyst can trace a root cause
Consolidates findings, then checks them against security standards
options: Amazon Macie
AWS Security Hub
Amazon Detective
Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Inspector
questions.explanation: The dossier's one-liners decide every pair: GuardDuty detects by correlating CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs with threat intelligence and machine learning; Inspector scans EC2, container images and functions for CVEs and network exposure; Macie finds sensitive data in S3 with machine learning and pattern matching; Detective builds a behaviour graph for investigation; Security Hub aggregates and prioritises findings and checks them against standards (2.4, security service jobs). The mnemonic that stops swaps: GuardDuty detects, Inspector scans, Macie finds sensitive data, Detective explains, Security Hub aggregates. Sibling services lose on the verb: Trusted Advisor only advises and CloudTrail only records, so neither builds a behaviour graph or scans for CVEs.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 - Deploying and operating in the cloud
questions.question: A checkout service's 95th-percentile latency crosses a threshold your team configured in your own account, and you want a notification plus an automated recovery action. Which service should you use?
options: Amazon CloudWatch: an alarm on your metric with an SNS or EC2 action
AWS Health Dashboard - Service health view
AWS Trusted Advisor: cost optimization category
AWS CloudTrail: event history
questions.explanation: CloudWatch is the monitoring answer: alarms watch a metric against a user-defined threshold and fire actions on state change: SNS for notification, plus EC2 stop/terminate/reboot/recover, Auto Scaling, Lambda or an SSM OpsItem. AWS Health covers AWS's own service events, Trusted Advisor reports best-practice gaps, and CloudTrail records who called which API.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 - Deploying and operating in the cloud
questions.question: A company runs its web tier in AWS while a regulated data store remains in its own virtualized data centre, and both sides are operated as one estate. Which cloud deployment model best describes this?
options: Public cloud, because part of the workload runs in an AWS Region
Private cloud, because part of the estate is dedicated to a single organization on premises
Hybrid cloud, because it seamlessly integrates the company's public and private clouds
Multi-cloud, because two infrastructure platforms are involved
questions.explanation: AWS defines hybrid cloud as an IT infrastructure design that seamlessly integrates a company's public and private clouds, and hybrid management 'can be done using services from a single cloud provider'. Two platforms alone do not make multi-cloud: multi-cloud requires services from different THIRD-PARTY cloud providers (two or more public providers). Private cloud describes only the on-premises half, and public cloud describes only the AWS half.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 - Deploying and operating in the cloud
questions.question: A developer launches Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS and AWS Lambda and asks which service model each illustrates. Which mapping is correct?
options: EC2 = PaaS, RDS = IaaS, Lambda = SaaS
EC2 = IaaS, RDS = a managed database service where AWS patches the OS and database but application optimization stays with the customer, Lambda = abstracted service where AWS runs the OS and platform
EC2 = SaaS, RDS = PaaS, Lambda = IaaS
All three are IaaS because the customer still owns data and IAM in every case
questions.explanation: AWS categorizes Amazon EC2 as IaaS and says it 'requires the customer to perform all of the necessary security configuration and management tasks' (guest OS, software, security group configuration). For RDS the matrix gives AWS OS patching, database patching, backups, scaling and high availability, while application optimization stays Customer in every column. Lambda is abstracted: AWS manages the infrastructure, the OS and the application platform; the customer owns code, function IAM and data. Nothing here is SaaS - AWS states it does not offer SaaS services.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 - Deploying and operating in the cloud
questions.question: An audit finds that six months of console tweaks have left a running stack out of step with the CloudFormation template that created it. Which statements guide the team's remediation correctly?
options: Configuration drift means the configuration that provisioned the environment no longer matches the actual environment
Re-applying the template is the documented remedy, because the template is a text file the team can diff
Hand-editing the drifted resource back into place re-creates the drift at the next change
Manual resource creation is error prone, which is why template-managed environments stay repeatable and consistent
The team must delete the stack first, because CloudFormation cannot reconcile resources it did not just create
AWS CodeDeploy is the credited tool for detecting and repairing configuration drift
questions.explanation: The lesson defines configuration drift as the configuration that provisioned your environment no longer matching the actual environment, and the operating rule is to RE-APPLY THE TEMPLATE: the template is a text file you can diff, manual creation is error prone, and a hand edit of the drifted resource simply re-creates the drift. The delete-first option fails because deletion is how a stack removes the resources it created, not how drift is repaired; the stated remedy starts from the template you still have. The CodeDeploy option fails on scope: CodeDeploy sits on the out-of-scope list for CLF-C02, so a deployment-shaped name can never be credited (T3 naming trap).

questions.subdomain: 3.1 - Deploying and operating in the cloud
questions.question: A governance reviewer is ranking four deployment targets from the most infrastructure the customer must operate down to the least. Put them in the order the shared responsibility matrix gives, most customer responsibility first.
options: Amazon EC2: AWS owns hardware, power and cooling while the customer patches the guest OS
On-premises data centre: the customer carries all nine responsibility rows
AWS Lambda: AWS runs infrastructure, OS and platform; the customer owns code and IAM
Amazon RDS: AWS adds OS and database patching, backups, scaling and high availability
questions.explanation: AWS's nine-row matrix gives the customer 9 of 9 rows on premises, 6 of 9 on Amazon EC2 (AWS takes server maintenance, hardware lifecycle and power, network and cooling), 3 of 9 on Amazon RDS (AWS adds OS patching, database patching, backups, scaling and high availability), and the abstracted tier for Lambda where AWS runs the infrastructure, OS and platform. So the ladder is on-premises, then EC2, then RDS, then Lambda. Swapping EC2 and RDS fails because it reverses who patches the guest operating system, and putting Lambda before RDS fails because AWS takes strictly more of the stack on the abstracted tier than on the managed database tier; application optimization stays with the customer in every column, so it never reorders the ladder.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 - Deploying and operating in the cloud
questions.question: A platform lead is writing an access standard for the team. Match each situation to the AWS access route the deployment lesson prescribes for it.
prompts: One exploratory change made at 2 a.m. in the browser
The same change repeated monthly across 20 AWS accounts
A running application that creates its own bucket
A shell step wired into a CI pipeline
A custom tool that signs its own HTTPS requests
options: AWS SDK - the application calls AWS from its own code
AWS CLI - commands run inside a command-line shell
AWS Management Console - centralized service consoles
AWS API - signed HTTPS requests sent directly
Infrastructure as code - a reusable CloudFormation template
questions.explanation: Each pair is decided by one qualifier. Exploratory and urgent means one-time work in the AWS Management Console, which IAM calls the most common method. The same change every month across 20 accounts is repeatable, so a CloudFormation template is reused in a consistent and repeatable manner. A running application reaching AWS at runtime uses an AWS SDK, a shell step inside a pipeline uses the AWS CLI, and a custom tool that signs its own HTTPS requests uses the AWS API. A pre-authenticated browser shell would be AWS CloudShell, which is explicitly out of scope for CLF-C02 and therefore never earns credit here.

questions.question: A regulated workload must keep all personal data inside a specific national jurisdiction, and the business also wants low latency for local users. Which Region-selection factor takes priority?
options: Price: the Well-Architected cost pillar says to deploy in the cheapest Region available
Compliance and data residency: a stated legal boundary beats latency and price, with latency as the next consideration
Service count: always pick the Region with the most services regardless of jurisdiction
Opt-in status: only the 17 Regions enabled by default may hold regulated data
questions.explanation: The Region decision set is compliance/residency, latency, price, features and opt-in status: and a legal or regulatory boundary always wins. COST07-BP02 says the opposite of option A: deploy in higher-cost Regions only when latency, data residency or sovereignty requires it, because pricing differs due to land, fiber, electricity and taxes. Opt-in status determines visibility, not legality, and service availability is a constraint rather than a priority.

questions.question: A solutions architect is drawing the AWS global infrastructure for a new team. Which statement is correct as of Oct 2026?
options: Each AWS Region consists of a minimum of three isolated, physically separate Availability Zones, and 124 AZs span 39 launched Regions
Each AWS Region contains exactly one Availability Zone, and edge locations are additional Availability Zones in other countries
Availability Zones are physically the same site in every Region, and a Region is a single data centre
There are more Regions than Availability Zones because every Region must contain at least two Regions
questions.explanation: AWS states each Region has a minimum of three isolated, physically separate AZs, and its statistics block reports 124 AZs across 39 launched Regions as of Oct 2026 (plus announced plans for 7 more AZs and 2 more Regions in Saudi Arabia and Chile). Regions cluster multiple data centres, AZs are discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and physical security, and edge locations are delivery points: not AZs.

questions.question: An engineer claims to have deployed 'the application across 1,140 edge locations for maximum availability'. Which correction is accurate as of Oct 2026?
options: 1,140 is the number of AWS Regions with edge caches; availability is improved by adding more Regions

1,140+ refers to CloudFront's embedded PoPs inside ISPs: a delivery and caching layer you cannot deploy workloads into; availability comes from running across at least two Availability Zones (of the minimum three per Region)
1,140 is the Global Accelerator PoP count, and Global Accelerator provides availability by running EC2 instances
Edge locations are Availability Zones in other countries, so 1,140 edge locations means 1,140 AZs
questions.explanation: As of Oct 2026 the counts are: CloudFront 750+ PoPs (100+ cities, 50+ countries), 1,140+ embedded PoPs across 300+ cities, 15 Regional edge caches; Global Accelerator 130 PoPs; Route 53 about 93 locations counted from AWS's feature page (AWS publishes no official total). Edge locations deliver and cache: you cannot launch EC2 there: and workload availability is a job for multiple AZs within a Region.

questions.question: Two teams in different AWS accounts must place their instances in the same physical data centres, and an Application Load Balancer deployment keeps failing its subnet check. Which statements are correct as of Oct 2026?
options: AZ codes such as us-east-1a are account-relative, so one account's letter can be a different site in another account
AZ IDs such as euw1-az1 identify the same physical location in every account
The Application Load Balancer console requires subnets from at least two Availability Zones
AZ ID tables list 109 AZ IDs across the 34 standard Regions
us-east-1a names the identical physical data centre in every AWS account
Every account sees all 39 launched Regions with no opt-in step
questions.explanation: AZ codes are account-relative: accounts created before November 2025 see different physical data centres for the same letter, while an AZ ID such as euw1-az1 names the same physical location in every account, so a cross-account placement question is answered with AZ IDs. The load balancer check is real: the ALB console enforces subnets from at least two Availability Zones. As of Oct 2026 the AZ ID tables list 109 AZ IDs across the 34 standard Regions. The identical-site option fails because it asserts exactly what account-relative codes deny, and the all-39-Regions option fails twice: a standard commercial account sees 34 Regions (39 minus 2 GovCloud, 2 China and 1 European Sovereign), and only 17 are enabled by default while 17 must be opted into.

questions.question: A content team is tracing how a CloudFront delivery actually reaches a user and where the cache tiers sit. Order the steps as the global infrastructure lesson describes them, starting from the user's request.
options: On a cache miss the PoP fetches from your origin, possibly via a Regional edge cache
The user's browser asks DNS to resolve the site name
The origin returns the object and caches it for the next request
DNS resolves the user to the nearest point of presence
questions.explanation: The request path starts with the user asking DNS, then DNS resolves the user to the nearest point of presence, where a cache hit is answered by the PoP itself. On a cache miss the PoP fetches from your origin (Amazon S3, an ALB or a media origin), optionally one tier back through a Regional edge cache, and the origin caches the result for next time. Resolving after the fetch fails because the PoP cannot answer before DNS has pointed the user at it, and treating the Regional edge cache as the front door fails because those 15 caches sit inside a Region, one tier behind the edge PoPs, not in front of them.

questions.question: A network architect is mapping exam triggers to the right global-infrastructure component. Match each need to the component the lesson pairs it with, using the counts as of Oct 2026.
prompts: Deliver cached content from the nearest point of presence
Fail over fast on static anycast IPs with no DNS wait
Resolve a domain name and route by latency or failover
Run workloads in a fault-isolated unit with its own power
A delivery tier in front of the Regions where no EC2 runs
options: Amazon CloudFront - 750+ PoPs caching at the edge
Amazon Route 53 - global DNS with latency and failover routing
AWS Global Accelerator - 130 PoPs and static anycast IPs
Edge location - a point of presence in front of the Regions
Availability Zone - fault isolation with independent power
questions.explanation: CloudFront is the cache and CDN plane with 750+ PoPs that answer from the nearest point of presence and fetch from an origin on a miss. Route 53 is the DNS plane with latency, failover, geoproximity, weighted and IP-based routing, and its failover speed is bounded by the DNS TTL you configured. Global Accelerator is the anycast IP plane with 130 PoPs and static anycast IPs, so failover never waits on a DNS cache. The Availability Zone is the deployable fault-isolation unit inside a Region, minimum three per Region with independent power, cooling and physical security, while an edge location is a delivery point in front of the Regions where you cannot launch an EC2 instance. Confusing CloudFront with Global Accelerator fails because only CloudFront caches; confusing the edge location with an AZ fails because only the AZ is deployable.

questions.question: A company wants container orchestration with no cluster management fee and no worker nodes to patch, using the AWS-native orchestrator. Which combination is correct?
options: AWS Elastic Beanstalk with Amazon Lightsail: both are serverless container platforms
Amazon ECR with AWS Batch - ECR orchestrates and Batch stores the images
Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate: no orchestration fee, and Fargate removes node management
Amazon EKS with the EC2 launch type: EKS has no cluster fee and you patch nothing
questions.explanation: ECS is the AWS-native orchestrator and AWS documents no ECS management fee for Fargate or EC2 launch types; Fargate is the serverless compute engine that works with both ECS and EKS, billed per vCPU and per GB of memory per second with a one-minute minimum. EKS is managed Kubernetes and charges 0.10 USD per cluster per hour (standard support), ECR is an image registry rather than an orchestrator, and neither Beanstalk nor Lightsail is a serverless container platform.

questions.question: A data engineer sees the instance name `r7g.xlarge` and must confirm what it implies before launching. Which statement is correct?
options: R = memory-optimized family, 7 = generation, g = Graviton (Arm) processor, xlarge = size within the family
R = reserved instance, 7 = seven-year licence, g = GPU, xlarge = seven times normal memory
R = storage-optimized family, 7 = number of attached volumes, g = general purpose, xlarge = 4x large disk
R = running total, 7 = seven Availability Zones, g = glibc-only image, xlarge = extra network bandwidth
questions.explanation: AWS names instance types by [series][generation][options].[size]: the first position is the series (R = memory optimized), the second is the generation (higher = newer), the letter suffix is the option (g = Graviton), and everything after the dot is the size. Graviton changes both silicon and operating-system support, so m7i and m7g are not interchangeable.

questions.question: An Auto Scaling group is documented with a minimum size of four, a desired capacity of six and a maximum size of twelve. A scaling policy requests that capacity rise by eight instances. What happens?
options: The request fails and the group is deleted because min, desired and max are inconsistent
Desired capacity becomes fourteen, because policies override the maximum
Desired capacity is capped at twelve, because the maximum is a hard ceiling
The group terminates two instances to keep the ratio stable
questions.explanation: An Auto Scaling group attempts to maintain its desired capacity, but scaling policies only move desired capacity within the min/max bounds: six plus eight would be fourteen, so the group stops at the maximum of twelve. Minimum four is a floor, maximum twelve is a ceiling; both are respected, and unexpected terminations are replaced rather than causing the group to be deleted.

questions.question: A team is wiring an AWS Lambda function into an event-driven pipeline and asks which published limits and billing details it must design around. Which statements are correct as of Oct 2026?
options: Memory can be configured from 128 MB to 10,240 MB in 1 MB increments
The timeout defaults to 3 seconds and can be raised to a maximum of 900 seconds
Billing is 0.20 USD per 1 million requests plus GB-seconds rounded up to the nearest 1 ms
Always Free covers 1,000,000 requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month
The function runs for up to 15 minutes by default with no timeout change
AWS Lambda sizes a fixed cluster of servers in advance that the team then manages
questions.explanation: All four keyed statements are the lesson's dated Lambda figures: memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB in 1-MB steps, a 3-second default timeout with a 900-second ceiling, 0.20 USD per 1 million requests plus GB-seconds rounded to the nearest 1 ms, and an Always Free allocation of 1,000,000 requests plus 400,000 GB-seconds each month. The 15-minute option fails as a numeric bait: 900 seconds is the maximum a team can raise the timeout TO, while the default is 3 seconds, so nothing runs for 15 minutes without a configuration change. The fixed-cluster option fails on the service model: Lambda is serverless and event-driven, invoked directly or through event source mappings, with no servers to provision or manage.

questions.question: During a flash sale the operations team watches an Auto Scaling group absorb a traffic spike. Order the steps as the compute lesson describes them, from the metric crossing its threshold to traffic flowing.
options: The policy moves desired capacity inside the configured minimum and maximum
A traffic spike drives the watched metric past its threshold
The load balancer takes the new instance and sends traffic only to healthy targets
An instance launches from the launch template and passes its health check
The alarm on that metric fires and triggers the group's scaling policy
questions.explanation: The sequence is spike, alarm, policy, launch, traffic: the metric crosses its threshold, the CloudWatch alarm fires into the scaling policy, the policy moves desired capacity while respecting the configured minimum and maximum, an instance launches from the launch template (the required input for an Auto Scaling group) and passes its health check, and Elastic Load Balancing then routes traffic only to the healthy targets. Alarm before policy fails because the alarm is what triggers the policy, and traffic before registration fails because routing to an unready instance breaks the guarantee that the balancer sends traffic only to healthy targets; Auto Scaling decides HOW MANY instances exist, while the load balancer decides WHERE the traffic goes.

questions.question: A finance engineer is pairing each requirement with the EC2 purchasing option that satisfies it. Match them, using the commitment and discount figures as of Oct 2026.
prompts: Unpredictable spiky usage, no commitment, 60-second minimum
Batch work that can restart after a two-minute notice
Steady per-hour commitment that must follow the team across Regions
Bring-your-own-licence work priced per socket or per core
Capacity reserved in one specific AZ, billed whether used or not
Fixed configuration for 1 or 3 years plus AZ capacity reservation
options: AWS Savings Plans (Compute) - up to 66 percent off
Dedicated Host - whole-host billing exposing sockets and cores
Capacity Reservation - On-Demand price with no discount
On-Demand Instances - pay by hour or second, no commitment
Spot Instances - up to 90 percent off with a two-minute notice
Standard Reserved Instance - up to 72 percent off for 1 or 3 years
questions.explanation: Unpredictable usage with no commitment is On-Demand, which bills by the hour or second with a 60-second minimum. Interruptible batch work that can absorb a two-minute interruption notice is Spot, up to 90 percent off. A steady per-hour commitment that must survive changes of family, Region, operating system, Fargate and Lambda is a Compute Savings Plan, up to 66 percent off. Per-socket or per-core licensing is the Dedicated Host, billed per host with sockets and cores exposed. A reservation of capacity in one specific AZ at the On-Demand price, charged whether or not you use it, is a Capacity Reservation. And a fixed configuration for 1 or 3 years that must also reserve AZ capacity is a Standard Reserved Instance, up to 72 percent off. Two mix-ups fail: Compute Savings Plans give NO capacity reservation, and a Region-scoped Reserved Instance is a discount only, so an AZ requirement selects the options the stem names.

questions.question: A brand-new application has an unpredictable traffic pattern, no reliable usage history, and the team refuses to pay for throughput while the app is idle. Which DynamoDB configuration should they choose?
options: Provisioned capacity with auto scaling, because provisioned is always cheaper at this scale
Provisioned capacity with a target utilization of 100%, so no capacity is ever wasted
On-demand capacity mode, which bills a fixed hourly price whether or not traffic arrives
On-demand capacity mode: the default, billed per request, which scales to zero when traffic stops
questions.explanation: On-demand is DynamoDB's default capacity mode: you pay per request with no capacity planning, the table scales to zero so idle costs nothing, and it can burst instantly to twice the previous peak. Provisioned capacity bills RCU and WCU per hour whether they are used or not: the opposite of the stated requirement: and AWS recommends a 70% auto-scaling target rather than 100%, because a 100% target leaves no headroom for bursts.

questions.question: A company wants a relational database where AWS owns backups, software patching, automatic failure detection and recovery, while the company keeps responsibility for schema and application tuning. Which option matches AWS's own responsibility table?
options: On-premises hardware: AWS manages the facilities while the customer patches the engine
Amazon S3 with a SQL layer: AWS patches the engine and the customer owns nothing
Run PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2, AWS then owns patching and backups
Amazon RDS - AWS owns scaling, high availability, backups and database/OS patching, and the customer still owns application optimization
questions.explanation: In AWS's published comparison, application optimization belongs to the customer in all three columns, while scaling, high availability, backups and database/OS patching belong to AWS for RDS and to the customer for both EC2-hosted and on-premises databases. AWS therefore recommends Amazon RDS as the default for most relational deployments. On EC2 you own patching and backups; on premises you own hardware and power too.

questions.question: An Amazon RDS primary is at 95% CPU because a reporting job runs heavy SELECTs every night. Management proposes enabling Multi-AZ to fix it. What is the BEST response?
options: Enable Multi-AZ and add a second standby, because standbys double read capacity
Do nothing: Multi-AZ also scales reads, so the proposal already works
Enable Multi-AZ: the standby replica absorbs the read traffic automatically
Create a read replica and point the reporting job at it, because a Multi-AZ standby serves no read traffic
questions.explanation: AWS states directly: 'The high availability option isn't a scaling solution for read-only scenarios. You can't use a standby replica to serve read traffic. To serve read-only traffic, use a Multi-AZ DB cluster or a read replica instead.' A Multi-AZ instance standby replicates synchronously and exists only for failover; a read replica replicates asynchronously and accepts SELECTs, which is what the reporting job needs.

questions.question: A bank is planning a low-downtime exit from an on-premises Oracle database to Aurora. Order the migration steps as the database lesson lays them out, starting with schema conversion.
options: AWS DMS creates source and target endpoints and runs the initial load
AWS SCT converts the Oracle schema and PL/SQL procedures to PostgreSQL
The application switches to Aurora once replication lag is effectively zero
The SCT assessment report flags the objects a human must rewrite
DMS keeps replicating ongoing changes while replication lag is watched
questions.explanation: The lesson's sequence is convert, then move, then cut over: AWS SCT converts the schema and code from one database engine to another and its assessment report lists what it cannot convert, so a human rewrites those objects next. AWS DMS then creates source and target endpoints, performs the initial load, and keeps replicating ongoing changes; once lag is effectively zero the application switches to Aurora. Skipping SCT fails because DMS alone leaves unrunnable SQL in the target, and cutting over before replication settles fails because ongoing changes would still be missing; SCT without DMS leaves an empty target, which is why the conversion step cannot be the whole migration.

questions.question: A data team is choosing a datastore for five workloads. Match each requirement to the service the database lesson names for it.
prompts: Petabyte dashboards aggregating three years of sales
A shopping cart that must cost nothing while idle
A rate limiter needing TTLs, sorted sets and automatic failover
Fraud ring traversal from account to device to IP and back
A MySQL order system needing AWS-managed patching and backups
options: Amazon Neptune - managed graph database for traversals
Amazon RDS - managed relational engine with AWS backups
Amazon Redshift - columnar OLAP warehouse for analytics
Amazon ElastiCache - in-memory store with Redis OSS
Amazon DynamoDB - NoSQL in on-demand capacity mode
questions.explanation: Aggregating years of history at petabyte scale is OLAP, so Amazon Redshift, the columnar warehouse filed under Analytics with Spectrum for files in Amazon S3. A cart with unpredictable spikes, no joins and zero idle cost is Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode, which scales to zero and bills per request. TTLs, sorted sets and automatic failover belong to Amazon ElastiCache with the Redis OSS or Valkey engine; a fraud ring traversed account to device to IP is a graph walk, so Amazon Neptune; and a MySQL order system that wants AWS to own patching, backups and Multi-AZ failover is Amazon RDS. Two near misses fail: Redshift omits OLTP features such as efficient single-row manipulation, and ElastiCache is an ephemeral cache that is never the system of record.

questions.question: A team is sizing Amazon Aurora for a 120 TiB relational estate with a heavy read tail and wants to know which published behaviours it may design around. Which statements are correct as of Oct 2026?
options: The single cluster volume auto-grows to 256 TiB and is independent of the database instances
Aurora is compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL and provisions through the RDS console, CLI and API
The cluster supports up to 15 Aurora Replicas reading from the shared volume
I/O-Optimized becomes worth switching to when I/O spending is 25 percent or more of Aurora DB spend
Failover takes about five minutes because three Availability Zones must re-synchronise
Storage grows only in manual 10 GB steps that the team must request
questions.explanation: Those four statements are the dossier's dated Aurora facts: one cluster volume replicated across three Availability Zones, independent of the instances, auto-growing to 256 TiB; MySQL and PostgreSQL compatibility provisioned through the same RDS console, CLI and API; up to 15 Aurora Replicas; and the 25 percent I/O-spend rule for I/O-Optimized. The five-minute failover option fails on numbers: AWS reports failover typically under 60 seconds and often under 30 seconds, with replica rebuild typically under 10 minutes, so five minutes is invented. The manual 10 GB option fails as a sibling-service trap: the 10 GB storage step belongs to Amazon DocumentDB, and even there growth is automatic rather than requested, while Aurora's own storage simply auto-grows.

questions.question: A financial workload requires a dedicated private connection to an on-premises data center with consistent bandwidth, bypassing internet service providers in the network path. Which service should the architect select?
options: AWS Site-to-Site VPN: two IPsec tunnels established over the public internet in minutes
AWS Direct Connect: a dedicated private connection with consistent bandwidth
AWS Client VPN: a managed remote-access VPN for individual users
AWS Transit Gateway: a hub that interconnects VPCs and on-premises networks
questions.explanation: Direct Connect is the dedicated private link that bypasses ISPs and provides consistent bandwidth; note that it is NOT encrypted by default. Site-to-Site VPN is the fast, always-encrypted, best-effort option with two tunnels of up to 1.25 Gbps each. Client VPN serves individual laptops, and Transit Gateway is the many-VPC-plus-on-premises hub rather than a dedicated point-to-point circuit.

questions.question: A private subnet must read objects from Amazon S3 with no internet gateway, no NAT gateway and no public IP addresses, at zero hourly and zero per-GB endpoint charge. Which option fits?
options: An interface endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon S3 in each Availability Zone
A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, whose route is added to the subnet's route table, with no hourly charge and no per-GB charge
A NAT gateway in the public subnet plus an internet gateway route
A VPC peering connection with a VPC that already has internet access
questions.explanation: Gateway VPC endpoints are available only for Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB, require no internet gateway or NAT device, and cost nothing hourly or per GB. Interface endpoints charge roughly 0.01 USD per hour per Availability Zone plus 0.01 USD per GB processed, NAT gateways add both an hourly and a per-GB charge, and peering never provides edge-to-edge internet access.

questions.question: Instances in a private subnet must download operating-system patches, but nothing on the internet must be able to reach those instances. Which design meets the requirement?
options: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC and add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway in the private subnet's route table
Place a NAT gateway with an Elastic IP in a public subnet and point the private subnet's 0.0.0.0/0 route at it, giving outbound-only access
Assign public IPv4 addresses to the instances and open port 22 in their security group
Peer the private VPC with a third VPC that has internet access, using edge-to-edge routing
questions.explanation: A NAT gateway is outbound-only: external services cannot initiate a connection with the private instances, while the instances can still reach the internet. Adding an internet gateway route would make the subnet public, assigning public IPv4 addresses exposes the instances, and peering never grants edge-to-edge access: a peer cannot borrow another VPC's internet gateway.

questions.question: Two application teams have built separate VPCs and propose relaying traffic through a third VPC so that the three networks behave as one fabric. Which statements about that design are accurate as documented?
options: A peering connection is strictly one-to-one, and transitive peering relationships are not supported
Overlapping CIDR blocks cannot be peered, and a peer cannot borrow your internet gateway
A peering request that nobody accepts expires after 7 days
Creating a peering connection charges an hourly fee for as long as the connection exists
A peer VPC can route through your NAT gateway, giving the pair edge-to-edge internet access
AWS Transit Gateway is charged 0.01 US dollars per attachment-hour
questions.explanation: The dossier's peering facts make the first three statements true: peering is a strict one-to-one relationship with no transitive peering, overlapping CIDRs are rejected, there is no edge-to-edge (a peer cannot use your internet gateway, NAT gateway, VPN, Direct Connect or gateway endpoint), and an unaccepted request expires after 7 days. The hourly-fee option fails because creating the peering connection is free; only cross-AZ data transfer through it bills, at 0.01 US dollars per GB with same-AZ transfer free. The NAT gateway option is the responsibility flip the lesson warns about: NAT is outbound for your own subnets and never a service a peer may borrow. Transit Gateway bills 0.05 US dollars per attachment-hour (about 36.50 US dollars per month), so 0.01 is the numeric bait attached to a true service name.

questions.question: Match each traffic-shaping requirement to the Amazon Route 53 routing policy that implements it: five trigger phrases teams routinely mix up:
prompts: Active-passive service with a health check on the primary
Canary release sending 10 percent of traffic to a new build
Reply with up to eight healthy records picked at random
Send each user to the Region that serves them lowest latency
Route by the country the requester IP address resolves to
options: Weighted routing
Latency routing
Failover routing
Geolocation routing
Multivalue answer routing
questions.explanation: Route 53 has exactly eight routing policies and each has one trigger phrase: active-passive plus a health check on the primary selects failover; in the proportions that you specify (canary and A-B splits) selects weighted; up to eight healthy records returned at random selects multivalue answer, a DNS-level alternative to a load balancer; multiple Regions with best latency selects latency; and the location of your users selects geolocation. The plausible mix-ups fail on their qualifiers: geoproximity routes by the location of your resources with a bias, not by the requester country; simple routing is one resource with no health check, so it cannot do active-passive; and multivalue cannot replace Elastic Load Balancing when the stem asks for path-based routing or connection draining.

questions.question: A Linux application needs a boot volume, sustained database IOPS, and the ability to snapshot for restore. Which block-storage answer is correct?
options: Instance store, because it offers the highest local I/O and survives an instance stop
An st1 throughput-optimized HDD volume, because HDD is always the cheapest boot option
A gp3 volume for boot plus io2 where a provisioned IOPS ceiling is required, backed by incremental snapshots
An S3 Glacier Deep Archive mount, because archive classes can be attached to EC2
questions.explanation: gp3 is the default boot-capable SSD with 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any volume size; io1/io2 (io2 Block Express up to 256,000 IOPS, 99.999% durability) answer a mission-critical IOPS ceiling. Snapshots are incremental and AWS does NOT automatically back up EBS volumes. Instance store loses all data when the instance is stopped and cannot be snapshotted, st1 and sc1 cannot be boot volumes, and S3 cannot be mounted as a block device.

questions.question: An operations team needs to overwrite-and-audit objects, automatically delete expired ones, and make sure deleting an object does not destroy its history. Which combination delivers that?
options: Enable versioning for history, add a lifecycle rule with expiration and noncurrent-version expiration actions, and rely on delete markers instead of hard deletes
Enable replication only, because replication deletes old versions automatically
Turn off encryption, because encrypted objects cannot be expired
Use S3 One Zone-IA, which stores a second copy in another AZ
questions.explanation: Versioning can never be reversed once enabled, a delete only adds a delete marker so prior versions remain, lifecycle expiration actions delete expired objects on your behalf and NoncurrentVersionExpiration clears old versions (every version is billed in full). Replication requires versioning on both ends and replicates deletions, so it is not a backup; encryption state is irrelevant to expiry and encrypted objects stay encrypted; One Zone-IA uses one AZ, not two.

questions.question: Data-lake objects have an unknown and changing access pattern, and the team refuses to pay per-gigabyte retrieval fees. Which S3 storage class fits?
options: S3 Standard-IA, because infrequent access is always cheaper
S3 Glacier Deep Archive, because it is the cheapest class overall
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which moves objects automatically and charges no retrieval fees
S3 One Zone-IA, because one Availability Zone reduces cost without affecting durability
questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering is designed for unknown or changing patterns: objects move to Infrequent Access after 30 days and to Archive Instant after 90 days, with no retrieval fees and only a small per-object monitoring charge. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA both charge retrieval fees and both require a 30-day minimum storage duration; Deep Archive is the cheapest but requires up to hours to restore; and One Zone-IA keeps 11-nines durability while dropping availability to 99.5% by using a single AZ.

questions.question: A marketing team wants to publish a static brochure site from Amazon S3 and asks an architect to confirm the defaults, the public-access posture and the HTTPS story. Which statements are accurate?
options: An S3 static website needs an index document, Block Public Access turned off and a public-read s3:GetObject grant
S3 static websites serve only HTTP endpoints, so HTTPS requires a CDN such as Amazon CloudFront
SSE-S3 has been the default encryption configuration for every bucket since 5 January 2023 at no extra charge
A new bucket starts open to the internet, because public access is an opt-out setting
SSE-KMS reuses the S3 default key, so it never adds a key charge
The bucket Region can be changed later, because only the bucket name is global
questions.explanation: All three keyed statements come straight from the storage dossier: a static website requires an index document plus Block Public Access off and a public-read s3:GetObject grant; static websites support only HTTP endpoints, so HTTPS needs CloudFront in front; and SSE-S3 has encrypted every new object by default since 5 January 2023 at no extra cost. The open-by-default option reverses the real posture, because a bucket is private by default with Block Public Access on and ACLs off. The SSE-KMS option is numeric bait: SSE-KMS adds per-key cost, SSE-C brings your own key, and only SSE-S3 is free. The Region option fails because a bucket Region is fixed at creation even though the globally unique name suggests otherwise, which is why the exam's Region choice comes before the bucket is created.

questions.question: Match each file requirement to the AWS service that satisfies it: the file and gateway answers this exam expects:
prompts: Lift and shift a Windows file server with AD and NTFS permissions
One NFS file system mounted by hundreds of Linux containers
NFS and SMB from a single engine for a mixed protocol team
An on-premises share whose saved files land as S3 objects
A virtual tape library that archives to Glacier over time
options: Amazon EFS
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon S3 File Gateway
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway
questions.explanation: Each prompt carries the qualifier that picks its service: Windows with Active Directory and NTFS ACLs is FSx for Windows File Server; a POSIX NFS file system shared by many Linux containers is Amazon EFS, which is Regional across at least three Availability Zones; NFS plus SMB from one engine is FSx for NetApp ONTAP; a local share whose files become S3 objects with the path as the key is the S3 File Gateway; and a virtual tape library archiving into Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive is the Tape Gateway. The traps are layer and scope errors: Amazon EFS is not supported with Microsoft Windows, so it cannot answer the lift-and-shift prompt, and FSx for Lustre is on the out-of-scope list, so no option may credit it even though it is a real FSx engine.

questions.question: A support team wants the sentiment and key phrases of thousands of free-text tickets, with no ML experience. Which in-scope service fits?
options: Amazon Comprehend, a natural language processing service that finds sentiment, entities and PII in text
Amazon SageMaker AI, because every ML task requires building a model
Amazon Textract, because the tickets contain unstructured text
Amazon Rekognition, because it analyses support content
questions.explanation: Comprehend is the NLP service for sentiment, entities, key phrases and PII in text: no ML expertise required. Rekognition handles images and video, Textract extracts text, handwriting and data from scanned documents, and SageMaker AI is for building, training and deploying your own models rather than calling a pre-trained API.

questions.question: Analysts need ad-hoc ANSI SQL directly over objects in Amazon S3, with cost proportional to the data actually read. Which service and cost driver apply?
options: Amazon Quick Sight at 3 USD per user per month for each analyst
Amazon EMR at a per-second rate with a one-minute minimum
AWS Glue at 0.44 USD per DPU-hour, because SQL over S3 requires an ETL cluster
Amazon Athena at 5.00 USD per terabyte scanned, with a 10 MB minimum per query
questions.explanation: Athena is serverless ANSI SQL over S3 priced per query at 5.00 USD per TB of data scanned with a 10 MB minimum, and DDL plus failed queries cost nothing (as of Oct 2026). Glue catalogs and transforms rather than answering SQL, EMR is a cluster you operate, and Quick Sight is the dashboard layer on top: none of them bills by data scanned.

questions.question: A media company needs labels for uploaded photos, a chatbot on its support site, and an in-house model that forecasts churn from its own transaction history. Which statements are accurate?
options: Amazon Rekognition labels and detects objects in the uploaded images and video
Amazon Lex builds the conversational interface and is the technology that powers Amazon Connect
The churn forecast should call a pre-trained API instead of training a model
Amazon SageMaker AI is where the team builds, trains and deploys its own model
Amazon Q is the service chosen to build a custom forecasting model from company data
Amazon Textract labels objects in the uploaded video frames
questions.explanation: The dossier's ML tiering rule decides every option: images go to Rekognition (computer vision), the chatbot goes to Lex (conversational interfaces, and the same technology behind Amazon Connect), and a model built from the company's own data goes to Amazon SageMaker AI, whose AWS wording is build, train and deploy ML models. The pre-trained-API option inverts the rule for this third need, because a custom forecast on proprietary data is the build-your-own case, while the pre-trained tier covers Rekognition, Comprehend, Textract, Transcribe, Translate, Polly and Lex. Amazon Q is generative-AI assistants (Q Business and Q Developer), not a modeller, so it cannot own the churn model. Textract extracts text, handwriting and data from scanned documents; it never labels video frames.

questions.question: A product team is building a serverless analytics path for clickstream records, from the moment the application writes a line to the moment an executive sees a chart. Put the documented pipeline in order and drop the step that does not belong:
options: AWS Glue crawlers catalog the landed objects as tables
Amazon EMR provisions a Hadoop cluster to clean the raw records
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams receives the ordered event log
Amazon Athena runs SQL over the cataloged tables
Amazon Data Firehose batches records and writes them to Amazon S3
Amazon Quick Sight builds the executive dashboard
questions.explanation: The documented serverless analytics pipeline is: records are produced, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams receives them in ordered shards, Amazon Data Firehose batches and writes them to Amazon S3 with no consumer code to write, an AWS Glue crawler catalogs the objects as tables, Amazon Athena runs ANSI SQL over that cataloged data, and Amazon Quick Sight draws the dashboard. Amazon EMR is the step that does not belong: it is a managed Hadoop, Spark, Hive and Presto cluster you operate for big-data processing, and it is not part of this documented chain, so leaving it out is what the ordering tests. Skipping the Glue step is the classic failure, because Athena can only query tables it can see and the Glue Data Catalog is how it sees them, while Glue itself never answers a query.

questions.question: Match each language, speech or document task to the pre-trained AI service that performs it, with no model training:
prompts: Pull text, handwriting and form fields out of scanned pages
Turn a recorded podcast into timestamped written text
Narrate a training video in a lifelike synthetic voice
Localise the help centre into other languages on demand
Flag entities and sensitive details inside chat transcripts
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Translate
Amazon Textract
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Polly
questions.explanation: Each prompt names its data type, and the dossier's rule is never to swap the data type: scanned pages with handwriting and form fields go to Amazon Textract; audio to written text goes to Amazon Transcribe; written text to lifelike speech goes to Amazon Polly; on-demand translation between languages goes to Amazon Translate; and sentiment, entities, key phrases and PII in text go to Amazon Comprehend. The near-misses fail on the same axis: Comprehend cannot read a scanned page's layout, Textract does not listen to audio, and Transcribe produces text rather than speech, so it cannot narrate the video. All five are in-scope purpose-built AI services you call with your data, which is exactly why no SageMaker AI model appears in this list.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor's events must trigger a Lambda function only when a specific field matches, and a batch job must run nightly at 02:00 UTC. Which service and which documented limits apply?
options: Amazon SNS, because topics support cron expressions and up to five subscriptions
AWS Step Functions, because one state can wait until 02:00 UTC
Amazon SQS, because long polling can wait up to 20 seconds for a schedule
Amazon EventBridge: a rule can have up to five targets, there are up to 300 rules per event bus, and scheduled rules are handled by EventBridge Scheduler
questions.explanation: Content-filtered JSON events, SaaS partner sources and schedules are EventBridge's job: a single rule can send an event to up to five targets, an event bus holds up to 300 rules, and AWS steers scheduled rules to EventBridge Scheduler with 14,000,000 free invocations per month. SNS has no cron, Step Functions is for multi-step processes, and SQS long polling is a 20-second receive wait, not a scheduler.

questions.question: A developer claims a standard Amazon SQS queue processes every message exactly once, in the order it was sent. Which correction is accurate?
options: Standard queues give at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering, while FIFO queues give exactly-once processing with strict FIFO order
Both queue types guarantee exactly-once delivery; FIFO only adds strict ordering
Standard queues are exactly-once and FIFO queues are at-least-once
Both types are best-effort and ordering is always the caller's responsibility
questions.explanation: AWS documents standard queues as at-least-once delivery where a message may be delivered more than once, with best-effort ordering, and FIFO queues as exactly-once processing with strict order plus a 5-minute deduplication interval. Duplicates on standard queues are expected, so consumers must be idempotent.

questions.question: A company must present the output of its virtual machines on staff laptops and tablets without shipping hardware, and it wants a browser-only option for contractors. Which statements are accurate?
options: Amazon WorkSpaces delivers fully managed persistent virtual desktops to end users
Amazon AppStream 2.0 streams desktop applications to any browser or device without rewriting code
Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser keeps HTML and document object model data off the local machine
AWS Amplify presents virtual desktop sessions inside a browser tab
Amazon WorkDocs supplies the in-scope virtual desktop for the contractors
Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser transmits the document object model to the user device
questions.explanation: The end-user-computing stem in the dossier is verbatim: the services that present the output of virtual machines on end-user machines are Amazon AppStream 2.0 for applications, Amazon WorkSpaces for full desktops, and Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser for browser only, and that hosted browser transmits no HTML, document object model or sensitive company data to the local machine. AWS Amplify fails on category: it creates and deploys frontend web and mobile applications, so it builds the client rather than presenting a virtual machine. Amazon WorkDocs fails on scope: it is explicitly out of scope, and the in-scope storage and enablement rows never credit it. The last option is a straight contradiction of the Secure Browser guarantee, which is the claim the exam tests when a stem mentions contractor access.

questions.question: A warehouse team wants a StockUnavailable line in its application log to become a notification to the on-call channel. Order the documented chain from the log line to the delivered message and ignore the step that is not part of it:
options: An Amazon SNS topic delivers the notification to subscribers
AWS Health reports a service disruption in the Region
A CloudWatch alarm evaluates the metric and changes state
A log event arrives in the CloudWatch Logs group
A metric filter counts matching log lines and emits a metric
questions.explanation: The dossier documents the chain as log event, metric filter, alarm, then SNS action: the line lands in a CloudWatch Logs group, a metric filter turns matching lines into a metric such as OutOfStockError, the alarm evaluates that metric and changes state, and the alarm action publishes to an Amazon SNS topic that reaches email, SMS, HTTP or Lambda subscribers. AWS Health is the step that does not belong, because it answers is AWS's stuff working rather than is my application working, so it never sits inside your own log-to-notification path. Order matters too: the alarm cannot evaluate a metric the filter has not yet emitted, and the SNS topic is only reached after the alarm acts, which is why actions fire on state change rather than on every breaching minute.

questions.question: Match each delivery or diagnostic need to the in-scope service that answers it, using the 2026 task 3.8 categories:
prompts: Compile source code and run unit tests in the build stage
Trace a request across microservices for 30 days
Hold a workflow that waits three days for human approval
Build and deploy a frontend web or mobile application
Connect field devices that speak MQTT or HTTP to the cloud
options: AWS X-Ray
AWS Amplify
AWS CodeBuild
AWS IoT Core
AWS Step Functions
questions.explanation: Each prompt maps to one documented task 3.8 answer: AWS CodeBuild compiles your source code, runs unit tests and produces artifacts, billed per build minute with 100 free minutes per month; AWS X-Ray is distributed tracing, segments to traces to a service graph, with trace data retained 30 days; AWS Step Functions Standard runs up to one year with exactly-once execution, which is what a three-day human approval wait needs; AWS Amplify creates and deploys frontend web and mobile applications; and AWS IoT Core is the managed gateway that connects devices over MQTT or HTTP. The plausible alternatives fail on layer: an Amazon SQS delay tops out at 15 minutes and a three-day wait is not a queue's job, AWS CodePipeline models the release stages rather than compiling code, and Amazon WorkSpaces presents desktops instead of connecting devices. Also note the 2026 Developer Tools row holds only AWS CLI, AWS CodeBuild, AWS CodePipeline and AWS X-Ray, so older rosters naming CodeStar or Cloud9 are superseded.

questions.question: A team stops their Amazon RDS database every night to save money, but the bill barely moves. Which statement explains the remaining charges?
options: Stopped RDS instances are billed for provisioned storage and backup storage: only DB instance hours stop
RDS bills a 10-minute minimum for every stop and start operation performed
RDS converts the instance to Spot pricing while stopped, which is not cheaper
Backup storage is free for the first 12 months regardless of account age
questions.explanation: AWS states that while a database instance is stopped you are charged for provisioned storage and backup storage, but not for DB instance hours. Instance billing runs in 1-second increments with a 10-minute minimum while running, but that minimum is not what generates the stopped-instance charge: and longer backup retention simply increases it.

questions.question: Which combination gives BOTH a discount and a guaranteed capacity reservation in a specific Availability Zone?
options: A Compute Savings Plan plus an On-Demand instance
An On-Demand Capacity Reservation purchased at a discounted rate
A Standard Reserved Instance scoped to a specific Availability Zone
A Spot Instance fleet spread across three Availability Zones
questions.explanation: Only an AZ-scoped Standard Reserved Instance delivers both: the discount (up to 72% as of Oct 2026) and the capacity reservation. Savings Plans reserve nothing; an On-Demand Capacity Reservation reserves AZ capacity but bills at the full On-Demand price with no discount; Spot capacity can be reclaimed at any time.

questions.question: Which statement BEST captures AWS's general pricing principles in AWS's own sequence?
options: Pay a fixed annual contract, then negotiate volume rebates annually
Pay as you go, pay for what you use, pay less as you use more, and pay even less when you reserve capacity
Pay upfront for all capacity, then receive credits for unused hours
Pay per user seat, with discounts applied only by enterprise agreement
questions.explanation: AWS's How AWS Pricing Works whitepaper (published 24 February 2023) states exactly that sequence, and the live pricing page adds that pay-as-you-go works 'without requiring long-term contracts'. The three cost drivers are compute, storage and outbound data transfer, with inbound transfer free of charge.

questions.question: A platform team is forecasting egress for a new media pipeline, and its finance lead asks which statements about AWS data-transfer billing hold true as of October 2026. Which statements are correct?
options: Data transferred into AWS from the internet is free of charge
The free outbound allowance is granted separately to every AWS Region
Traffic between two services inside one Availability Zone costs nothing
Data transferred out to the internet is billed at one flat rate
Inter-Region outbound transfer draws on its own separate free allowance
questions.explanation: Inbound transfer from the internet is never charged, and traffic between services in the same Availability Zone is free, so those two statements are the correct pair. The outbound allowance is 100 GB per month aggregated across all AWS services and all Regions (excluding the China Regions and GovCloud), not granted per Region, so the second option is numeric bait (T6) on a true figure. Outbound transfer is tiered per GB - us-east-1 steps down as monthly volume rises - so the flat-rate option fails on structure, and Inter-Region outbound transfer is billed per GB out of that same global allowance rather than a second free pool.

questions.question: A team must choose an EC2 purchase option for several unrelated workloads and decides to walk AWS's purchase-option decision tree. Put the tree's branches in the order the tree visits them.
options: Steady and predictable workloads committed for one or three years
A temporary lab, a course exercise or a first prototype
Guaranteed launch room in a single Availability Zone
Fault-tolerant work that can be interrupted safely
Everything else with an unknown or short-lived pattern
questions.explanation: The tree opens with the free, no-risk branch: a temporary lab, learning exercise or first prototype goes to the Free Tier, which never answers a production-workload question. Next comes fault-tolerant, interruptible work, which is Spot (repriced about every 5 minutes, up to 90 percent off). Only then does it consider a steady, predictable workload needing a 1- or 3-year commitment: Standard Reserved Instance or EC2 Instance Savings Plan up to 72 percent, Compute Savings Plan or Convertible RI up to 66 percent. Guaranteed room in a single Availability Zone sits after the discount decision because an On-Demand Capacity Reservation grants no discount and bills whether the capacity is used or not; everything left over falls to On-Demand, the baseline with zero percent discount. The plausible wrong order - buying the deepest-discount commitment first - fails because the tree clears the free and interruptible options before any multi-year commitment.

questions.question: Match each monthly billing pattern an S3 or RDS owner reports to the charge dimension that explains it:
prompts: Bytes held in an S3 storage class during the month
A PUT request sent to an S3 bucket
Objects pulled back from an infrequent-access class
An Amazon RDS instance switched off for the month
options: Requests per 1,000; DELETE and CANCEL are free
Only instance hours stop; storage keeps billing
Storage in GB-month, priced by storage class
Retrieval per GB plus a minimum storage duration
questions.explanation: Every S3 storage class bills in GB-month at its own monthly rate, so stored bytes match the storage dimension. A PUT is a request charge counted per 1,000 requests, and DELETE and CANCEL requests are free while LIST bills at the PUT rate, so the PUT matches the request dimension. Reading data back out of an infrequent-access or archive class adds a per-GB retrieval charge plus a minimum storage duration, so retrieval is the third match. The stopped RDS instance is the trap: only DB instance hours stop, while provisioned storage and backup storage keep billing - and a stopped EC2 instance is no different, because EBS volumes, snapshots and data transfer continue. The second plausible miss is pricing GET at the PUT rate: GET and HEAD are far cheaper than PUT, COPY, POST and LIST.

questions.question: Requirement: notify the finance channel at 80% of a 50,000 USD monthly budget AND automatically prevent the creation of additional resources if the budget is breached. Which combination satisfies it?
options: AWS Cost Explorer with a forecast alert and an SNS topic
AWS Budgets with a threshold notification plus a budget action that applies an IAM policy denying provisioning
An SCP alone, because SCPs cap spending
The Cost and Usage Report delivered daily to S3
questions.explanation: AWS's documented pattern is to notify at 80 percent of the budgeted amount and apply an action: for example a custom IAM policy that denies provisioning additional resources. Budget actions can run programmatically or with approval and can apply IAM policies, SCPs or AWS resources, integrating with AWS Chatbot. Cost Explorer explores and forecasts but never enforces; an SCP can deny provisioning actions yet it cannot watch a spend target or notify anyone; the CUR is only an export.

questions.question: You need the PDF invoice, the tax lines and the issued-versus-pending status of this month's AWS bill. Which page do you open?
options: The Bills page
Payment preferences
AWS Cost Explorer default report
The Billing dashboard Home page
questions.explanation: The Bills page holds the bill summary (Issued vs Pending), payment information, charges by service (drillable to Region), charges by account (management account only), downloadable PDF invoices, savings and taxes. Home is the exploratory widget view, Cost Explorer answers 'why did cost move', and Payment preferences is where you change method or currency.

questions.question: A finance lead asks what actually changes when five subsidiary accounts move under AWS Organizations with consolidated billing. Which statements about that change are correct as of October 2026?
options: AWS treats every account as one account when it applies volume tier thresholds
A Reserved Instance bought by one account can discount other accounts' usage
AWS Marketplace charges land on the same consolidated bill
Support fees are pooled and charged once for the whole organization
Consolidated billing adds a separate monthly fee on top of usage
Each member account reaches volume thresholds on its own bill
questions.explanation: AWS treats all accounts in an organization as a single account, so member accounts do not reach tier thresholds individually - pooling is correct. Consolidated billing shares volume discounts, Reserved Instance discounts and Savings Plans across accounts, so an RI bought by one account can discount another account's usage - correct. AWS Marketplace usage is billed on the same invoice because one bill covers each seller of record - correct. Support is the documented exception: AWS calculates support fees independently for each member account and each account subscribes independently, so pooled support fails. Consolidated billing carries no extra fee as of October 2026, so the surcharge option fails, and the last option is a responsibility flip: it restates pre-consolidation behaviour, since aggregation is per service and every month starts at zero.

questions.question: A cloud finance analyst wants to split last month's shared platform spend between two product teams using a single tag. Put the required steps in the order they must happen.
options: Activate the user-defined tag as a cost allocation tag
Restructure the organizational units so each team is billed separately
Tag every billable resource with one consistent key
Group last month's spend by that tag in Cost Explorer
Wait up to 24 hours for the tag to reach cost data
questions.explanation: The tag must exist on every billable resource first, with one consistent key. Second it is activated as a cost allocation tag - and activation lives in the management account or a standalone account, because member accounts cannot activate tags. Third, allow up to 24 hours for the activated tag to start flowing into cost data. Fourth, group by that tag in Cost Explorer, or read it in the Cost and Usage Report, then reconcile against the Bills page. The restructure option is the trap: AWS states your bill will not reflect the structure you have defined in your organization, so adding or reshaping OUs never splits spend - activated cost allocation tags or cost categories do. Expect an untagged row too: resources tagged after the fact and non-tagging services never appear under the key.

questions.question: Match each cost-management question a team asks to the AWS tool that answers it:
prompts: Estimate a three-tier application before it is built
Send raw hourly line items to a bucket you control
Explain a bill increase, filtered by Region
Alert the team when forecast spend passes a target
Split Marketplace monthly fees that tags cannot cover
options: AWS Cost and Usage Report, daily CSV or Parquet to your bucket
AWS Budgets, notifications by email or Amazon SNS
AWS Pricing Calculator, free and needs no AWS account
AWS Cost Explorer, filter by service, Region and tag
Cost categories, since tags cannot allocate monthly fees
questions.explanation: Estimating an application that does not exist yet is the Pricing Calculator: a free web tool that needs no AWS account, assumes 730 hours in a month and does not assume the Free Tier, while Cost Explorer reads actual usage. Raw hourly line items delivered at least daily to your own S3 bucket in CSV or Parquet is the Cost and Usage Report, which carries both unblended and blended rates. Explaining a movement by Region, service or tag is Cost Explorer, whose console clicks are free (only API calls are billed) and whose data reflects usage up to the previous day. A threshold alert is AWS Budgets: monitoring and notifications are free, but an alert is a notification, not a cap - stopping spend needs a budget action. Finally, subscription-based charges such as AWS Support and AWS Marketplace monthly fees cannot be allocated by tags, so the escape hatch is a cost category.

questions.question: A customer on the Basic Support plan suffers a production outage and wants to escalate to AWS immediately. Which statement is correct?
options: Basic includes a designated Technical Account Manager
Basic includes the full Trusted Advisor check set, so the case is unnecessary
Basic cannot open technical support cases: it covers billing and account help, quota increases, forums, documentation and service health
Basic includes a first response within 1 hour for production system down
questions.explanation: Customers with the Basic Support plan cannot open technical support cases. What Basic does include, 24x7, is billing and account support, quota increases, forums, documentation and service health: plus Trusted Advisor core checks (all accounts get 56 free checks). Response-time ladders and TAMs only exist on plans that can open technical cases.

questions.question: Which statement about AWS Trusted Advisor availability is correct as of Oct 2026?
options: Customers on the Basic Support plan get no Trusted Advisor checks at all
Business Support+ includes TA Priority as well as the full check set
Trusted Advisor is available only on Enterprise Support, including TA Priority on every plan
All AWS accounts get 56 checks, Business Support+ unlocks the full set, and TA Priority is reserved for Enterprise and Unified Operations
questions.explanation: All AWS accounts get 56 Trusted Advisor checks and Business Support+ and above unlock an additional 426 (482 total on AWS's check page, which elsewhere advertises 'more than 500'). Basic gets core checks: including all Service Limits checks and selected Security and Fault tolerance checks: so 'no checks at all' is false. TA Priority is an Enterprise and Unified Operations feature, not a Business Support+ one.

questions.question: A production team is comparing the four support plans in the 2026 lineup before renewing. Which statements about those plans are correct as of October 2026?
options: Business Support+ has a published monthly minimum of 29 USD per account
Enterprise Support includes a named Technical Account Manager
Business Support+ handles technical cases by phone, web and chat 24x7
Unified Operations carries a monthly minimum of 5,000 USD
Enterprise Support gives a first response under 5 minutes for a business-critical outage
Developer Support is available for new subscriptions as of October 2026
questions.explanation: Business Support+ costs a 29 USD monthly minimum per account with a 30-day minimum commitment and answers technical cases 24x7 by phone, web and chat, so the first and third statements hold. Enterprise Support includes a Technical Account Manager, so the second statement holds. The traps: the 50,000 USD monthly minimum with a 90-day commitment belongs to Unified Operations while Enterprise is 5,000 USD, so that option swaps in the Enterprise figure against the wrong plan (T6 numeric bait); the 5-minute first response comes from a Unified Operations Incident Management Engineer while Enterprise commits to under 15 minutes for a business-critical system down (T4 over-claim); and Developer Support stopped taking new subscriptions after 2 December 2025 and is discontinued 1 January 2027, so it is the stale-version trap. First response is a response, not a resolution, and AWS commits only to every reasonable effort.

questions.question: During an incident, a team follows the five-step drill used to decide whether the fault is theirs or AWS's. Put the steps in the order the drill walks them.
options: Check the CloudWatch alarm state for your own metric
Review Trusted Advisor for gaps in your own configuration
Subscribe to the AWS Health API before starting the triage
Open service health to look for a public AWS service event
Open your account health for account-specific issues
Raise a case in the AWS Support Center as the last resort
questions.explanation: Step 1 is CloudWatch: is my own metric breaching? Step 2, only if that is green, is Health service health, the public view that needs no sign-in and shows events that are not specific to an AWS account. Step 3 is Your account health for account-specific issues and scheduled changes. Step 4 is Trusted Advisor, when the gap is in my own configuration - it advises only and never enforces. Step 5 is a Support Center case, where the severity I choose sets the first-response clock, and on Basic Support no technical case can be opened at all. The Health API option is not a step: the dashboard is free for all customers while the AWS Health API requires Business Support+ (receiving health events through Amazon EventBridge is free), and skipping straight to step 5 fails on a free plan.

questions.question: Match each request a team needs to send to the AWS channel that actually handles it:
prompts: Ask a general how-to question such as tagging 400 instances
Report someone reselling a stolen machine image
Record a workload review with high-risk issues and milestones
Open an account-and-billing case about our own invoice
Have a partner open technical cases for our account
options: AWS Support Center console for account cases
AWS re:Post, the AWS managed community
AWS Partner-Led Support on an eligible plan
AWS Well-Architected Tool, available at no cost
AWS Trust and Safety team, separate from support
questions.explanation: A general how-to question belongs on AWS re:Post, the managed community with the Knowledge Center articles - it is not for time-sensitive or account-specific questions. Abuse such as a stolen image being resold goes to the AWS Trust and Safety team, which is separate from AWS Support. A workload review that captures high-risk issues, an improvement plan and a milestone is the Well-Architected Tool, and that tool costs nothing. An invoice problem with our own account is an account-and-billing case in the Support Center - Basic Support can open billing and account cases around the clock even though it cannot open technical cases. Partner-Led Support lets an eligible partner open cases on our behalf; Professional Services and solutions architects are engagement offerings, not case channels.
